title: Estimate Gap
context: Grade 4, the closing topic of the chapter. An adult sees rounding done twice and then a subtraction. What is actually being taught is what an estimate is for. It is not a worse answer and it is not a guess: it is a fast answer whose job is to say whether the worked answer is anywhere near believable, and it earns its keep exactly when a trade has gone wrong and the worked answer is out by a whole thousand while looking perfectly neat on the line.

writeup.why: Get a quick answer by rounding both numbers first, then use it to decide whether the answer you worked out can be right.
writeup.look: A stage split down the middle, the exact working in columns on one side and the rounded numbers on the other, with a bar drawn between the two answers.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Estimate Gap' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many of the two numbers have been rounded against how many there are, two numbers side by side in ink, and under them the place both are going to, written in words rather than in figures; on the last two phases it carries the two answers, the estimated one in rose above the worked one in green. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The working area is split down the middle at x 607 by one ruled line that runs its whole height, and the two sides never borrow each other's room. The place picker runs along the top, three keys 180 by 48 at 64,202, at 258,202 and at 452,202, reading nearest hundred, nearest thousand and nearest ten thousand, with the chosen one standing proud of the other two; it moves both numbers as one piece, and an attempt to send them to different places lights both strips and asks again rather than doing it. The exact side is 520 by 214 at 64,266: a trade strip 32 tall across its top where a lending digit is struck through once with its smaller value written above it and the ten it lent is drawn arriving in the column it went to, a heading row 34 tall of six ruled cells reading L, TTh, Th, H, T and O, the greater number 48 tall in deep blue, the number being taken away 48 tall in amber with a minus to the left of its row, a rule 4 tall, and the answer row 48 tall in green. The estimate side is the same rectangle at 630,266 with no columns drawn in it at all, which is the whole point of it: the two rounded numbers are printed large in rose one under the other with their trailing zeros in grey, a rule is drawn under the lower one, and the estimated answer stands in rose beneath the rule. A number line strip 470 by 52 runs under each rounded number, at 654,396 and at 654,460, stretched so that the two nearest multiples of the chosen place sit on label plates at its ends with a halfway tick 4 by 36 between them and its value printed above it, and a drawn pin marking the number where it belongs on the line; the shorter of the two distances from the pin fills amber the moment both are drawn, so the nearer end is seen before a single digit is read. The gap bar is 1086 by 72 at 64,530, drawn only when both answers are standing: it runs along a line drawn from nothing up to the worked answer, touches both answers, and carries how far apart they are printed at its middle, in ink rather than in either answer's colour so that neither answer owns it. The judge bay is 1086 by 64 at 64,620, a slot 420 wide at its left holding an answer somebody else has written, room beside it for the estimate to build, and two keys at its right reading could be right and go back and work it again; the bay never marks the written answer, it draws the bar and asks which of the two the child would go back to. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across, with a thirteenth key that writes a run of zeros so a rounded number or an estimate can be finished in one press. On the third phase a strip of three place words, hundred, thousand and ten thousand, sits under the keys, because the place both numbers are going to is named before either of them moves. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the greater number on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, the answer under the rule is green, the ten lifted out of a column is vermilion and is always drawn small above the column it arrives in, a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, and a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading over it before it is told by its band, and a trade is told by the strike through the lending digit and by the smaller value written above it.
writeup.finish: The card shows one pair estimated and worked exactly, side by side, with the gap between the two answers still drawn and labelled.

phases.win: the estimate lands without a single column being written
phases.does: rounds both numbers and takes one rounded number off the other
phases.goal: the rounding happens before anything is taken away
phases.says: Round each number first, then take away. Not the other way round.
phases.check: Estimate 8,470 take 3,620 to the nearest thousand. Which did you do first, the rounding or the taking away?
phases.feels: the taking away turns out to be the easy half, and all of the work is in the rounding that comes first
phases.hands: Write the two numbers on squared paper, write the rounded number under each one, and only then draw the minus and take one rounded number off the other.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of your two numbers is already rounded? Second rung, the phase's: which two thousands is the other one sitting between? Third rung: the estimate side is cut to one number and its strip, and that number is rounded on its own before the other comes back. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: rounding once at the end is less work than rounding twice at the beginning, and the answer is the thing the question seems to be about.
wrong.move: works the exact subtraction first and rounds the answer afterwards, handing that in as the estimate.
wrong.screen: the two roads are drawn side by side on the estimate side with the order of their steps numbered beside them. On 5,623 and 2,365, rounding first gives 6,000 and 2,000 for an estimate of 4,000, while working first gives 3,258 and rounding that afterwards gives 3,000. Both are printed, neither is crossed out, and the question's own wording is lit above them.

wrong.why: the first number was the one being worked on, and the second looked ready to use just as it was.
wrong.move: rounds the greater number, leaves the smaller one standing exactly as it is, and takes that off the rounded one.
wrong.screen: the number line strip opens under the number that was left alone, stretched so that the two nearest thousands sit on plates at its ends with the number pinned between them; the estimate side takes rounded numbers only, so that number waits out on its strip until it is sent to one end or the other. On 6,987 and 5,698 the pin on the second strip stands nearer the upper end, so it goes to 6,000 and the estimate is 1,000 against a worked answer of 1,289. Nothing already written is cleared.

phases.screen: two numbers with the estimate side empty and the place already set
phases.soWhat: Round both numbers first and then take one rounded number off the other, which needs no columns at all because they both end in zeros.

phases.win: the gap bar is drawn short and labelled, and both answers stay standing
phases.does: runs the gap bar and reads how far apart the two answers are
phases.goal: the estimate sits near the exact difference rather than on it
phases.says: Put the two answers beside each other. How far apart are they?
phases.check: Your estimate is 1,000 and your worked answer is 728. Is your estimate wrong, and would you say the same if the worked answer had been 13,860?
phases.feels: near is what was asked for, and then a pair turns up where near is not very near at all
phases.hands: Work the subtraction exactly on the left of a page and estimate it on the right, then rule a line between the two answers and write on that line how far apart they are.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: were you asked for a worked answer or a quick one? Second rung, the phase's: how far apart are your two answers, and how big is the answer they are measuring? Third rung: the gap bar is laid along the length of the worked answer, so the distance is read against the size of the number it belongs to. Both answers stay on the stage.

wrong.why: an answer that does not match the right answer has been a wrong answer every time until now.
wrong.move: calls the estimate wrong because it does not equal the worked answer.
wrong.screen: the two answers drop onto one number line together, the worked 3,133 and the estimated 3,000 that 7,899 and 4,766 give, and the space between them is drawn and labelled 133; the line runs the whole length of the worked answer, so the gap is seen against what was being measured rather than on its own. The two rounding moves are printed beside it, 7,899 going up by 101 and 4,766 going up by 234, and 234 less 101 is the 133 that was left over. Both answers stay standing.

wrong.why: every pair worked so far has come out close, and a thing that has always happened stops being watched.
wrong.move: decides from one close pair that an estimate always lands near, and stops looking at the gap at all.
wrong.screen: the pair 10,900 and 10,172 is loaded beside the one just finished and both gap bars are run at once. The first is 133 long against a worked answer of 3,133. The second is 272 long against a worked answer of 728, because the greater number was pushed up by 100 and the smaller was pulled down by 172, and 100 and 172 together are the 272. Neither bar is marked right or wrong and both stay drawn.

phases.screen: both sides finished with the gap bar waiting between them
phases.soWhat: An estimate is meant to land near the worked answer and not on it, and how near it lands depends on which way each of the two numbers was rounded.

phases.win: the picker moves both strips together and the two rounded numbers land at the same place
phases.does: tries to round the second to a different place, then sets them both together
phases.goal: rounding to different places makes the estimate useless
phases.says: One went to the nearest thousand. Can the other go somewhere else?
phases.check: Round 7,480 and 2,360 both to the nearest thousand and estimate. Now tell me why sending one of them to the nearest hundred instead would spoil it.
phases.feels: one pair of numbers and two different estimates, and both of them survive
phases.hands: Round the same pair to the nearest hundred on one line and to the nearest thousand on the line underneath, and read the two estimates straight down the page.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what place are both of your numbers going to? Second rung, the phase's: which two round numbers of that size is each one sitting between? Third rung: the picker is cut to one place and both strips stretch to match it together, so neither can be sent anywhere on its own. The place words stay open under the pad.

wrong.why: rounding is the job that was asked for, and one round number looks about as useful as another.
wrong.move: sends the greater number to the nearest thousand and the smaller one to the nearest hundred, taking each to whichever place looks tidiest.
wrong.screen: both strips open together under the two numbers with the same place marked on each, and the picker is shown moving the two as one piece. On 7,480 and 2,360 the mixed rounding gives 7,000 less 2,400, which is 4,600 and answers no question that was asked, while sending both to the nearest thousand gives 7,000 less 2,000, which is 5,000 against a worked answer of 5,120. All three numbers are left standing and none is crossed out.

wrong.why: two different answers to one question have meant a mistake every time so far.
wrong.move: says the estimate made at one place must be wrong because it does not match the estimate made at another.
wrong.screen: two strips open together under the same number, one stretched to the hundreds either side of it and one to the thousands either side, with the same pin standing on both; the nearer end is a different number on each strip, and on each strip it really is the nearer end. The exercise this chapter closes on never names a place at all, and the worked case printed directly above it goes to the nearest thousand, so the nearest thousand is the reading printed across the top of the stage and kept there for every pair in it. Nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the place picker with one number already rounded and the other waiting
phases.soWhat: Both numbers go to the same place or the estimate means nothing, and where a question does not name a place, the worked case beside it names it.
phases.concept: Both numbers, and the same place

phases.win: the gap bar stretches long and the written answer is sent back to be worked again
phases.does: builds the estimate and decides whether the written answer can stand
phases.goal: an answer far from its estimate is the one to work again
phases.says: Your estimate and this answer are far apart. Which one would you check first?
phases.check: Somebody works 8,204 take 3,679 and writes 5,525. Estimate to the nearest thousand and tell me whether that answer can stand.
phases.feels: a fast answer that is roughly right catches a worked answer that is badly wrong
phases.hands: Before working a subtraction out at all, estimate it in your head and write that estimate in the margin, then work the subtraction properly and read the margin back.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does your estimate say the answer should be near? Second rung, the phase's: how far from it is the answer standing in the bay? Third rung: the written working is lit one column at a time from the ones until the first column that disagrees is found. Nothing in the bay is ever marked right or wrong.

wrong.why: a subtraction that is set out tidily looks like a subtraction that has gone well.
wrong.move: trusts a written answer because its columns look neat, and never builds the estimate beside it.
wrong.screen: the estimate builds in a moment on the right, 9,215 going to 9,000 and 3,684 going to 4,000 for an estimate of 5,000, and the gap bar is run from there to the written answer of 6,531, with the 1,531 between them printed on it. The written working is left standing exactly as it was with all its columns showing, and when it is worked again the answer is 5,531, the tens and the hundreds each fetching a ten from the column on their left.

wrong.why: a wrong answer feels like work to be thrown away rather than work to be looked at.
wrong.move: sees the gap stretch long and rubs the whole working out to begin it again.
wrong.screen: the columns of the written subtraction light one at a time from the ones, and the first column whose digit does not agree with the rebuilt one is the only one left lit; on that working it is the thousands, which lent a ten to the hundreds on its right and was never left one less, so a nine went into the working where an eight belonged. The rest of the columns stay standing, and the gap bar shortens to nothing as that single column is put right. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the judge bay holding a written answer with the estimate building beside it
phases.soWhat: An answer far from its estimate is the one to go back to, and building the estimate to find that out costs almost nothing.
phases.concept: An estimate tells you when an answer cannot be right

writeup.delight: The second phase, the moment the gap bar is run twice. The first pair is 25,896 and 12,036: the worked answer is 13,860, the estimate is 14,000, and the two come down onto one line drawn from nothing up to the worked answer, where the 140 between them is a step so short it has to be labelled before it can be seen. Then 10,900 and 10,172 are loaded and the same bar is run again: the worked answer is 728, the estimate is 1,000, and the 272 between them is more than a third of the whole answer, so the bar runs off the end of a line the first pair had barely marked. The label roughly doubled and the bar changed out of all recognition, so the number that measures a gap and the size of that gap are both on the stage at once, and they are plainly not the same thing. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the two numbers stand in deep blue and amber down the exact side with its columns ruled and its answer row empty, the estimate side is blank, the place picker along the top is already set to the nearest thousand and locked, and a number line strip is drawn under each number on the right but not yet stretched. On the second both sides are finished, the worked answer in green and the estimated one in rose, and the gap bar lies between them drawn and unlabelled. On the third one number has been rounded and the other is waiting, with the picker unlocked. On the fourth the judge bay is open along the foot with somebody else's answer already in its slot and the estimate side empty beside it. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the number line strip under the greater number, or the place picker, or the empty label on the gap bar, gives one slow pulse while the voice says to round both numbers first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two numbers, any place, with both sides running, the number line strips open and the gap bar live. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on rounding before subtracting, comparing an estimate with the exact answer, rounding both to the same place, and judging a written answer.

observations.why: Numbers that end in zeros have nothing to fetch and nothing to lend.
observations.soWhat: An estimate is quick, and quick is the whole reason for having one.
observations.observe: The estimate landed with no column drawn on that side of the stage at all.

observations.why: Both numbers moved the same way, so most of the two moves cancelled and only the difference between them was left over.
observations.soWhat: The gap between an estimate and a worked answer is nothing more than the two rounding moves put together.
observations.observe: Rounding 7,899 up by 101 and 4,766 up by 234 left the estimate 133 under the worked answer, so 3,000 stood beside 3,133.

observations.why: The greater number was pushed up by 100 and the smaller was pulled down by 172, and both of those widen a gap rather than cancelling, so the estimate sits 272 above the worked answer.
observations.soWhat: An estimate is not always close, and it is furthest out when the two numbers sit near each other and round opposite ways. It is worth having even then, because an estimate that loose would still catch an answer out by a whole thousand.
observations.observe: On 10,900 and 10,172 the estimate came to 1,000 while the worked answer was only 728.

observations.why: A trade that draws the ten arriving and forgets to take it off the column on the left hands the answer an amount that was never there.
observations.soWhat: An estimate cannot tell me the answer, but it can tell me in seconds that an answer cannot be right.
observations.observe: A worked answer sitting a whole thousand from its estimate turned out to have a lending column that was never reduced.

source_tool.description: The stage is split down the middle. On the left the two numbers are worked exactly, on a ruled column mat with the trades drawn the way the rest of the chapter draws them. On the right the same two numbers are rounded first and the rounded numbers are taken one from the other, and that side carries no columns at all, because numbers ending in zeros do not need any. A number line strip runs under each number on the right, stretched so that the two nearest multiples of the chosen place sit at its ends with the number marked between them, so rounding stays a choice of the nearer one rather than a rule about a digit. A place picker at the top says which place both numbers round to, and it moves both together: rounding one to a different place than the other is not something the picker will do, and trying it lights both strips and asks again. When both sides are finished a gap bar is drawn between the estimated difference and the exact one and labelled with how far apart they are, short when they sit close and long when they do not. A judge bay takes an answer somebody else has written, builds the estimate beside it and asks whether the written answer can be right at all.
source_tool.art_direction: A split stage, exact working and estimate / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that untie themselves, a rule between the number taken away and the answer, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A subtraction is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the greater number on top, the two numbers aligned by their right ends, the minus sign to the left of the lower row, and a horizontal rule between that row and the answer. A bare line of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach taking away.

A trade is always drawn as both of its halves. The lending column keeps its digit, struck through once, with its new and smaller value written small above it, and the ten it lent is drawn arriving in the column on its right. A short arrow runs from the lending column to the receiving one, left to right, never the other way.

A check by addition is drawn under the subtraction it tests, and the total it comes to is set beside the number the working started from, so the two can be read against each other without anything being cleared.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The greater number on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, and the answer under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, and a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, so the two halves of one trade are told apart at a glance. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a lending column is told apart by the strike through its digit and by the smaller digit written above it before it is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the strip under each number again, and at which end it is nearer.
voice.onNext: New numbers. Send them both to the same place before anything else.
voice.opening: Round both numbers first. Then take one from the other.
voice.onFinish: A fast answer and a worked one, standing together with the gap drawn between them.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any two numbers, any place, both sides running and the gap bar live.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: Both numbers, and the same place
An estimate tells you when an answer cannot be right

placement.where: After one pair has been estimated on paper with the exact difference worked beside it. The tool is what keeps both answers standing at once and measures the distance, which a written page can only do by being read twice.

answer_key.rule: To estimate a difference, round both numbers to the same place and then take the smaller rounded number off the greater one. Round first and subtract second, because working first and rounding the answer is a different question. Both numbers go to the same place, or the two are changed by different amounts and the gap between them shifts. The greater number still goes first after rounding. An estimate is meant to land near the exact difference, never to equal it, and a worked answer sitting far from its estimate is the one to go back to.
answer_key.wrong: The number line strip reopens under each number with the two nearest multiples of the chosen place at its ends, so the nearer one can be seen before any rule is said. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.

hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.

hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Round 6,284 to the nearest thousand, which gives 6,000.
Round 2,715 to the nearest thousand, which gives 3,000.
Take one rounded number off the other: 6,000 - 3,000 = 3,000, and the exact difference of 3,569 sits near it.
items.question: Estimate 6,284 - 2,715 by rounding each number to the nearest thousand.
items.checkpoint: Rounding comes first and the taking away is done to the rounded numbers.
items.misconception: Working the subtraction first and rounding the answer, which is a different question.

steps: Rounded to the nearest thousand, 8,713 becomes 9,000 and 4,297 becomes 4,000.
So the estimate is 9,000 - 4,000 = 5,000, worked without a single column.
The exact difference is 4,416, so the gap bar between them is short.
items.answer: The estimate is 5,000 and the exact difference is 4,416, which sits close to it
items.question: Estimate 8,713 - 4,297 to the nearest thousand, then work the exact difference and compare the two.
items.checkpoint: An estimate is meant to land near the exact difference, not to equal it.
items.misconception: Calling the estimate wrong because it does not come to 4,416.

steps: Rounding to different places changes the two by different amounts, so the gap between them shifts.
That child gets 7,000 - 2,400 = 4,600, which answers no question that was asked.
Sent to the same place, 7,480 becomes 7,000 and 2,360 becomes 2,000, so the estimate is 5,000 against an exact 5,120.
items.answer: Both numbers have to go to the same place. To the nearest thousand the estimate is 5,000, and the exact difference is 5,120
items.question: A child rounds 7,480 to the nearest thousand and 2,360 to the nearest hundred, then subtracts. Why is that no use?
items.checkpoint: Both numbers are rounded to the same place, or the estimate means nothing.
items.misconception: Rounding each number to whichever place makes it easiest, one at a time.

steps: Round both numbers: 9,215 becomes 9,000 and 3,684 becomes 4,000, so the estimate is 5,000.
The written answer of 6,531 sits a whole thousand away from that, which is too far.
Working it properly gives 5,531, and the thousands column had fetched a ten that was never paid for.
items.answer: The estimate is 5,000, so 6,531 cannot be right. The exact difference is 5,531
items.question: A child works 9,215 - 3,684 and writes 6,531. Use an estimate to the nearest thousand to judge it.
items.checkpoint: An answer a whole thousand from its estimate is an answer to work again.
items.misconception: Trusting a worked answer because the columns look neat, instead of standing an estimate beside it.

items.final_answer: 4,000, because the rounded numbers are 6,000 and 2,000

items.question: Estimate 8,430 - 5,910 by rounding each number to the nearest thousand.

items.question: Estimate 7,624 - 4,180 to the nearest thousand, and give the exact difference as well.
items.final_answer: The estimate is 4,000 and the exact difference is 3,444

items.question: A child says an estimate of 4,000 must be wrong because the exact difference is 3,444. What would you tell the child?
items.final_answer: That an estimate is meant to land near the exact difference and not to equal it, and 4,000 does

items.question: Estimate 34,780 - 12,240 by rounding each number to the nearest thousand.
items.final_answer: 23,000, because the rounded numbers are 35,000 and 12,000

items.question: Why must both numbers go to the same place before they are subtracted?
items.final_answer: Because rounding them to different places changes the two by different amounts, so the gap between them shifts and the estimate is no use

items.question: A shop takes 62,410 one week and 27,865 the next. A till prints the difference as 3,455. Estimate to the nearest thousand and say whether the till can be right.
items.final_answer: The estimate is 34,000, and 3,455 is nowhere near it, so the till is wrong. The difference is 34,545

items.question: Estimate 20,850 - 20,130 to the nearest thousand, work the exact difference, and say whether the estimate was much use here.
items.final_answer: The estimate is 1,000 and the exact difference is 720, so the estimate is 280 out, which is a large slice of so small a difference; rounding pushed the two numbers apart

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: sets the place both numbers round to and moves the two together
rounds both numbers before anything is taken away
works the two numbers in columns with the trades drawn
takes one rounded number off the other, with no columns at all
shows a number between the two nearest multiples of the chosen place
draws and labels the distance between the estimate and the exact difference

teaching_notes: Round first and take away second, every time, and say it in that order out loud, because working first and rounding the answer is a different question that gives a different number. The closing exercise never says which place to round to, and the worked case just above it rounds to the nearest thousand, so read the whole exercise that way and say so, otherwise half the class will round to hundreds and be right about the method and wrong about every answer. Use the number line strips for the first few, because rounding read as a rule about a digit falls over the moment a number sits near the middle, and rounding read as a choice of the nearer multiple does not. Spend time on the pairs where the estimate lands badly. Where one number rounds up and the other rounds down, the estimate can sit a long way off, and a child who has only ever seen close estimates will start treating them as answers. Finish on the judge bay. This is where the whole chapter comes back round: a worked answer out by a thousand is almost always a lending column that was never reduced, and the estimate is what catches it in seconds.
generation_prompt: Build an estimating tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage split down the middle. On the left the two numbers are worked exactly on a ruled column mat with named headings, the greater number on top, and every trade drawn as a struck lending digit with its smaller value above it and the ten arriving in the column on its right. On the right the same two numbers are rounded first and the rounded numbers are subtracted with no columns at all. A place picker across the top selects the nearest hundred, thousand or ten thousand and rounds both numbers together, refusing to send them to different places and lighting both strips when that is attempted. A number line strip under each number on the right stretches so that the two nearest multiples of the chosen place sit at its ends, with the number marked between them. When both sides are finished, a gap bar is drawn between the estimated difference and the exact one and labelled with the distance, short when they sit close and long when they do not. A judge bay accepts an answer typed in from elsewhere, builds the estimate beside it and stretches the gap bar long when the two are far apart, sending that answer back to the exact side. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set the picker to the place the question asks for. Round both numbers first, then take one rounded number off the other. Work the exact answer on the other side. Run the gap bar between the two. If they are far apart, work the exact side again.
